title: The Distinction of an Inquiry-Based Conversation
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece draws a sharp line between advocacy-driven conversation and dialogue built on genuine inquiry. It argues that most workplace exchanges default to debate and persuasion because that mode is fast and familiar, even though it rarely produces real understanding. Dialogue, by contrast, requires leaders to treat their own understanding as incomplete and to use curiosity rather than argument to explore what others actually believe and feel. The piece offers a simple diagnostic: if a conversation ends and participants still can't articulate what others think or feel, dialogue never happened. It closes by framing inquiry as a discipline that must be practiced deliberately, since our instincts pull us toward advocacy instead.
points: Distinguishes advocacy/debate (fast, persuasion-focused) from dialogue (slow, inquiry-focused)
Names our default preference for snap judgments as the reason advocacy usually wins out
Offers a concrete test for whether real dialogue occurred in a conversation
Frames inquiry as a practiced skill rather than a natural tendency
quotes: That statement lies at the heart of honest exchange between people.
Because we are drawn to the simplicity of snap judgments and fast conclusions, pathways of advocacy and debate will commonly win out.
Dialogue is a distinct conversational form made identifiable by its focus on inquiry and exploration, as opposed to advocacy and persuasion.
A conversation guided by inquiry places importance on excavating meaning and exploring deeply what people believe and feel about a topic.
If the conversation comes to an end and team members can’t articulate what others believe and feel about an issue, topic, or decision, they haven’t engaged in dialogue.
You are my question and I am yours—and then there is dialogue.
